title: Characteristic sequence of a Borel quotient
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes are as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $X^*(J)=\operatorname{Hom}_{F\text{-grp}}(J,\mathbf G_m)$, with addition given by multiplication, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. A Borel subgroup means a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup; solvable means that iterating the derived subgroup scheme eventually gives the trivial group, and the derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. An invertible module on a scheme $Y$ is an $\mathcal O_Y$-module locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_Y$; $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$ is its group of isomorphism classes under tensor product. There exists a Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$. For every Borel subgroup $B$, the quotient $Q=G/B$ is represented by an $F$-scheme and the projection $q:G\to Q$ is a right $B$-torsor locally trivial for the Zariski topology: it admits local sections and $(g,b)\mapsto(g,gb)$ identifies $G\times_F B$ with $G\times_Q G$. For $\lambda\in X^*(B)$ let $c_B(\lambda)$ be the class of the line bundle $G\times^B\mathbf A^1$ on $Q$, defined by $(g,z)b=(gb,\lambda(b)^{-1}z)$; equivalently it is the descent of this $B$-equivariant trivial line on $G$. This is a homomorphism, and the sequence of abelian groups $$0\longrightarrow X^*(G)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}_B}X^*(B)\xrightarrow{c_B}\operatorname{Pic}(Q)\xrightarrow{q^*}\operatorname{Pic}(G)\longrightarrow0$$ is exact, meaning that the first map is injective, the last map is surjective, and at every intermediate term the image equals the kernel.

source.place: Theorem 18.15, sequence (128), printed p.390; its Borel-character form in the proof in section 18.f, printed pp.395-396; Borel existence and splitting recalled at section 18.c, p.390.

proof.text: There is a Borel subgroup: choose a smooth connected solvable closed subgroup of largest dimension, starting with the identity subgroup. A proper inclusion $B\subsetneq B'$ of such subgroups strictly increases dimension: $B'$ is an integral affine variety (by [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry] for $B'$ with its identity subgroup and $p=\mathrm{id}_{B'}$), so its proper closed subset $B$ has $\dim B\le\dim B'-1$ by [lem-wf-affine-dimension-drop]. Thus this choice is maximal. Fix any Borel $B$. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient] to $B\subseteq G$ to obtain $q:G\to Q$. Its test-scheme coset criterion gives the isomorphism $G\times_F B\to G\times_QG$: its inverse is $(g,g')\mapsto(g,g^{-1}g')$, with the second component factored through $B$ by that criterion. By [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry], $G,Q$ are smooth geometrically integral and regular Noetherian, $q$ is smooth and $G\times_Q\operatorname{Spec}L$ is nonempty and integral for every point of $Q$ and every field extension $L$ of its residue field, and $Q$ is proper. The group $B$ is split solvable by [lem-sfb-split-solvable-torsors-and-variety], so its torsor $q$ has Zariski local sections by that same statement.

source.place: Definition 17.6 and Theorem 17.9(a), pp.353--354; Section 18.f, final paragraph, p.396; Proposition 16.55(c), p.344.

proof.text: The action $(g,z)b=(gb,\lambda(b)^{-1}z)$ gives descent data on the trivial line on $G$: the cocycle is the identity $\lambda(b_1b_2)^{-1}=\lambda(b_1)^{-1}\lambda(b_2)^{-1}$. Since $q$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact, $\{q:G\to Q\}$ is an fpqc covering (each affine open of $Q$ is the image of finitely many affine opens of $G$), and [lem-pc-fpqc-descent] gives its descended invertible module $L_\lambda$. Multiplication of fibre coordinates identifies the descent data for $L_\lambda\otimes L_\mu$ with those for $L_{\lambda+\mu}$, and $L_0=\mathcal O_Q$, so $c_B$ is a homomorphism. The pulled-back bundle has the nowhere-zero frame $s_\lambda(g)=[g,1]$, hence $q^*c_B=0$. For any character $\chi$ of $G$, the function $t(g)=\chi(g)^{-1}$ obeys $t(gb)=\chi(b)^{-1}t(g)$; thus $g\mapsto[g,t(g)]$ descends to a nowhere-zero section of $L_{\chi|_B}$ by the same descent equivalence. Therefore $c_B\circ\mathrm{res}_B=0$.

source.place: Section 18.c, p.390, and proof of Theorem 18.32 at X(H), p.395; Stacks descent.tex Tag 023T for effective descent.

proof.text: First derive the normalized-unit observation from [lem-sfb-rosenlicht-product-unit-factorization]. For any smooth connected affine $F$-group $J$ and any unit $u:J\to\mathbf G_m$ with $u(e)=1$, apply its displayed identity to $v(x,y)=u(xy)$ on $J\times_FJ$ at $(e,e)$: it gives $u(xy)=u(x)u(y)$ as regular functions, so $u$ is a character. The integral hypotheses for $J$ follow from [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry] applied to the identity subgroup of $J$ with the quotient $p=\mathrm{id}_J$, which satisfies the test-point criterion and the lifting condition trivially. In particular, the observation applies both to $G$ and $B$. Also [lem-weil-pbc-proper-reduced-algclosed-global-sections-product] applied to the nonempty connected proper reduced scheme $Q$ gives $\Gamma(Q,\mathcal O_Q)=F$. If a character $\chi$ of $G$ is trivial on $B$, it is constant along $q$-fibres and its functions along Zariski local sections of $q$ glue to a unit on $Q$. This unit is constant, and its value at $q(e)$ is $1$, so $\chi=1$. Restriction is injective.

source.place: Propositions 12.48--12.49, pp.246--247; Section 18.f, pp.395--396, identification U(G)=X(G) and the initial zero.

proof.text: Suppose $c_B(\lambda)=0$. A nowhere-zero global section pulls back to $g\mapsto[g,t(g)]$ for a regular unit $t$ on $G$. In the associated bundle $[gb,z]=[g,\lambda(b)z]$, so the section condition is exactly $t(gb)=\lambda(b)^{-1}t(g)$. Apply the normalized-unit observation of the preceding step to $u(g)=t(g)/t(e)$: $u$ is a character of $G$. Putting $g=e$ in the section condition gives $u|_B=\lambda^{-1}$. Therefore $u^{-1}$ restricts to $\lambda$. Together with step 2 this proves $\ker(c_B)=\operatorname{im}(\mathrm{res}_B)$.

source.place: Theorem 18.32, exactness at X(H), p.395; Proposition 12.49, p.247.

proof.text: Let $L$ be an invertible module on $Q$ and suppose $q^*L$ has a global frame $s$. View $s(g)$ as a nonzero vector of $L_{q(g)}$. Over $G\times_F B$, the two frames $s(gb)$ and $s(g)$ have the same base point, so their ratio is a regular unit $a(g,b)$ with $s(gb)=s(g)a(g,b)$ and $a(g,e)=1$. By [lem-sfb-rosenlicht-product-unit-factorization], $$a(g,b)=a(g,e)a(e,b)/a(e,e)=a(e,b).$$ The frame identity applied successively to $b_1,b_2$ gives $a(e,b_1b_2)=a(e,b_1)a(e,b_2)$; hence $\lambda(b)=a(e,b)$ is a character of $B$. The map $(g,z)\mapsto s(g)z$ to the total space of $L$ is invariant under $(g,z)b=(gb,\lambda(b)^{-1}z)$. By full faithfulness in [lem-pc-fpqc-descent] it descends to an isomorphism $L_\lambda\simeq L$, since it is already an isomorphism after pullback to $G$. Thus $\ker(q^*)\subseteq\operatorname{im}(c_B)$; the reverse inclusion is step 2.

source.place: Theorem 18.32, exactness at Pic(X), pp.395--396; Remark 12.50, p.247.

proof.text: Let $M$ be any invertible module on $G$. Put $K=F(Q)$ and $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. A Zariski local section of $q$ on a nonempty open of the integral scheme $Q$ yields $G_\eta\simeq B_K$. By [lem-sfb-split-solvable-torsors-and-variety], every invertible module on $B_K$ is trivial, including $M|_{G_\eta}$. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-generic-trivial-line-descent] to $q:G\to Q$: the regular integral separated finite-type hypotheses and the smooth surjectivity with geometrically integral fibres were all obtained in step 1. We obtain an invertible module $N$ on $Q$ with $q^*N\simeq M$. Thus $q^*$ is surjective. Combining this with steps 2--5 proves the stated exact sequence at every term.
